Frances McDormand brings her trademark blend of intelligence, wit and emotional honesty to David Lindsay-Abaire's compassionate drama about class, loyalty and the choices that define us.
Smartly directed by Daniel Sullivan, the often-caustic production provides a humane, realistic and absorbing examination of ordinary people's behavior when their world is threatened.
In the current economy of scaled-back American dreams, when the role of class is too often dismissed, Good People has a quality rarely seen on Broadway: It seems necessary.
And discovering how Margie operates — and where she’s coming from — is one of the more subtly surprising treats of this theater season.
Like everything in this deceptively amiable, stealthily gripping tragicomedy, however, the words are less plain than they first let on.
Good People is a fine, small, heartfelt work that shadowboxes with social darkness in a safely lit room, floating on a vast sea of unsaid things.
Ms. Lindsay-Abaire has written a solidly crafted play that asks hard questions about class, loyalty and the meaning of success in contemporary America.

And McDormand captures all of Margaret's contradictions with sensitivity and depth, and the haggard, haunted look of a hamster that's spent too long on the treadmill but lacks the wherewithal and the means to stop.
But it's too thoughtful, moving and richly entertaining to be missed.
Good plays entertain, but "Good People" is even better, the kind that makes you think and feel as well.
Tate Donovan proves a fine foil as Mike, highlighting the character's conflicting feelings of relief at escaping a dead-end life and guilt at no longer being a true Southie.
Director Daniel Sullivan can’t finesse the play’s contrivances.

McDormand’s performance raises the stakes on Abaire’s drama, sparking moments of suspense amidst basically banal material.
